title: Soviet Jewry
hook: Jews in the Soviet Union are denied the right to practice or to leave

segments.voice: Yesterday, airlifts, and your line: on eagles' wings. Did you carry something for someone? A new week begins somewhere very different, behind a closed border. Day one thousand thirty.

Someone keeps an ear on the stairwell. In a kitchen in Moscow, late at night, curtains drawn, a handful of people lean over one worn Hebrew textbook, its pages typed and retyped and passed from hand to hand. Teaching Hebrew like this could cost a person their job, or worse. Every person at this table has asked the government for permission to leave for Israel, and every one has been told no. They have a name for themselves: refuseniks. Today's word.
screen: `A KITCHEN IN MOSCOW, CURTAINS DRAWN.` → `ONE WORN HEBREW BOOK.` → `EVERY ONE TOLD NO.`

segments.voice: In the Soviet Union, religion was officially discouraged, and Jewish life was squeezed hard. Synagogues were few and watched. Hebrew was difficult to learn. Jews often met suspicion at universities and at work. And for a long time, few were allowed to leave. Then some Jews began to apply anyway, to emigrate to Israel. Applications were refused, sometimes with a vague reason about state secrets, and the person who asked could lose their job just for asking. That's a refusenik: someone refused permission to leave. Some waited for years. Inside, they did what Jews had done under pressure before. They learned in secret, taught each other Hebrew, and kept the holidays quietly. On Simchat Torah, young Jews gathered outside a Moscow synagogue and danced in the street. Outside the country, Jews and non-Jews around the world took up their cause, with a slogan from Exodus. Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh and say: "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness." Notice the second half, the part a slogan can leave off. The demand isn't only to leave. It's to be free to worship, to hold the feast. That's the freedom this story keeps asking for: freedom to go, and freedom to be who you are where you stand. In time, the gates opened, and families left, some to Israel, some to America and elsewhere. Tomorrow, one refusenik who found a way to stay free inside a prison cell.
screen: `JEWISH LIFE SQUEEZED HARD.` · `REFUSED, AND PUNISHED FOR ASKING.` · `HEBREW IN SECRET KITCHENS.` · `LET MY PEOPLE GO, TO HOLD A FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: do one thing freely. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're free to do that someone, somewhere, is not: read a book of your choosing, learn a word of Hebrew, light a candle, say a blessing out loud, sit in silence without anyone checking. Choose one. Do it now, or plan it for today, slowly and on purpose, remembering the kitchens where it cost something. If you pray, you can do it as a prayer. The bell holds the time.
Refusenik. A Soviet Jew refused permission to leave, often punished for asking, who kept Jewish life going in secret. Today's word.
Your line: let my people go. Today, notice one freedom you use without thinking, and use it once on purpose. Day one thousand thirty.

howItsDone: Jews retell the story of the refuseniks alongside the Exodus, and 'Let my people go' from Exodus 5:1 became the slogan of the worldwide movement for Soviet Jewry.
